TL;DR What is […] The post Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0 , an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. TL;DR Size: 753B parameters (MoE, ~40B active per the GLM-5.3 base), 1M-token context, 128K max output. Runs on: 8 GPUs with SGLang (tested); NVFP4 for NVIDIA B200/B300, MXFP4 for AMD MI350X/MI355X. Performance: Beats GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research; roughly matches Kimi-K3 on GPQA-Diamond. Best: 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research vs 33.3% for GPT-6-Astra (self-reported). Worst: Trails GPT-6-Astra (max thinking) by 3.33 points on NMR structure elucidation. What is Hydrogen-1.0? Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. How was Hydrogen-1.0 trained? The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Domain knowledge: chemistry, materials science and life sciences data. Research scenarios: task-specific feedback from Deep Principle scientists. Laboratory records: full-cycle electronic lab notebook records captured through Mira . Discovery trajectories: sequences of choices and feedback, including failed attempts. Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. How does Hydrogen-1.0 perform on benchmarks? On public benchmarks, Deep Principle reports Hydrogen-1.0 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research. The tweet thread from one of the founders’ report 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond. That improves on GLM-5.3 and roughly matches Kimi-K3, per the blog. Internal research-task evals compare it with GPT-6-Astra at maximum thinking: Scientific computing: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 5.13 percentage points. Forward reaction prediction: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 4.76 percentage points. NMR structure elucidation: GPT-6-Astra leads by 3.33 points. In transition metal complex design, models chased a larger HOMO-LUMO gap over 5 rounds. By round 5, Hydrogen-1.0 reached a mean best-so-far gap of 4.318 eV. GPT-6-Astra reached 3.689 eV and Kimi-K3 reached 3.353 eV. On 117 experiment-planning questions, Hydrogen-1.0 scored above Kimi-K3. GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5.5 were excluded after refusing more than 50% of requests. What can it do in a real lab workflow? The technical post shows 4 demos . Hydrogen-1.0 writes Python to build a polyethylene melt and runs GROMACS. It detects a topology error, repairs it, and analyzes the corrected 40 ns trajectory. It grows an Ireland-Claisen reaction network of 27 structures through 30 plausible reactions. It ranks 7 candidate monoformylation products of 2-bromonaphthalene from a 1H NMR trace. It also writes a JSON protocol for a 12-vial Suzuki coupling study. A virtual lab compilation step catches an aspiration without a fresh tip before execution. How do you deploy Hydrogen-1.0? Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Deep Principle team tested BF16 serving with SGLang on 8 GPUs using tensor parallelism of 8. NVFP4 targets NVIDIA B200 and B300. MXFP4 targets AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with a reasoning_effort setting. It reports 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research, above GPT-6-Astra’s 33.3%. Training adds lab records and discovery trajectories, not just papers. It reads a git-based site and its market, then opens pull requests for SEO, GEO and conversion work. The post The Letter Company Releases Letterpress-1: A Coding Agent Built for Growth Engineering appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Letter Company has released the beta of Letterpress-1 , a coding agent, harness and IDE for growth engineering. The Letterpress-1 coding agent reads a website and its market, then decides what should exist. It builds the change in a sandbox and opens a pull request with a live preview. TL;DR Size: Letter team says it combines frontier models with fine-tuned small models; names and sizes are not disclosed. Runs on: Letter’s hosted platform against your git repository. No local GPU needed. Setup takes under 5 minutes, per Letter. Performance: No public benchmark. Letter shows 1 self-reported, side-by-side page build against Codex. Best: 760 tools exposed through 1 registry over MCP, REST and CLI. Worst: No measurable eval; entry plan is $100/month with overage at 5x the list rate. What is Letterpress-1? Letterpress-1 is a growth engineering agent from The Letter Company. It turns site and market signals into pull requests. The letter company team argues that websites, unlike apps, react to outside forces. These include agent behavior, Google rankings, human visits and competitor activity . General coding agents were built to scale codebases, not to act on those signals. The agent is aimed at teams that host their marketing site in git. It is proactive: it suggests the next thing to build. Examples include de-anonymization, landing pages, warmed emails, blog automation and agent telemetry. How does Letterpress-1 work? Letterpress-1 runs in 3 modes : Build: create a page or feature from a prompt, with brand copy and visuals kept consistent. Plan: pick a goal and get a build plan of growth actions. Fix: find site issues and dispatch pull requests to fix them. Every change follows the same loop. The agent reads the site, plans and builds in a sandbox. It reviews its own change, then opens a pull request. Each change returns a preview link of your own site . Nothing lands until you choose a preview, a pull request, or a merge after checks pass. Letter team lists 6 surfaces. These are the web platform, a Slack app, the letterpress CLI and a website portal. A standalone app and your own agent round out the list. The in-site IDE works on a live page. Press ⌘L, edit text where you see it, and a pull request follows. Showcase examples also cover A/B tests from live edits. For developers, agents.md documents an MCP server at app.letterstory.com/api/mcp with OAuth. The MCP manifest, OpenAPI spec and API reference form 1 registry of 760 tools. Claude Code, Codex or any MCP-capable agent can call the same functions the app uses. What are Proofs, Simulations, Benches and Phantoms? The launch post highlights 4 primitives aimed at winning over AI agents as buyers: Proofs: signed evidence of customer success, built from telemetry and billing data, for agent visitors. Simulations: mirror versions of your API or MCP with simulated data, so agents can try before buying. Benches: self-hosted, reproducible benchmark apps with open-source code and independent governance. Phantoms: independent, autonomous blogs used to sandbox growth strategies. The site adds more: Kernels, Letterbases, Visitors and Mailers. Then it watches competitor sitemaps and flag new pages. Letter team positions these as replacements for tools like G2, Semrush, Profound, RB2B and Instantly. It reads a git-based site and its market, then opens pull requests for SEO, GEO and conversion work. The post The Letter Company Releases Letterpress-1: A Coding Agent Built for Growth Engineering appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> The Letter Company has released the beta of Letterpress-1 , a coding agent, harness and IDE for growth engineering. The Letterpress-1 coding agent reads a website and its market, then decides what should exist. It builds the change in a sandbox and opens a pull request with a live preview. TL;DR Size: Letter team says it combines frontier models with fine-tuned small models; names and sizes are not disclosed. Runs on: Letter’s hosted platform against your git repository. No local GPU needed. Setup takes under 5 minutes, per Letter. Performance: No public benchmark. Letter shows 1 self-reported, side-by-side page build against Codex. Best: 760 tools exposed through 1 registry over MCP, REST and CLI. Worst: No measurable eval; entry plan is $100/month with overage at 5x the list rate. What is Letterpress-1? Letterpress-1 is a growth engineering agent from The Letter Company. It turns site and market signals into pull requests. The letter company team argues that websites, unlike apps, react to outside forces. These include agent behavior, Google rankings, human visits and competitor activity . General coding agents were built to scale codebases, not to act on those signals. The agent is aimed at teams that host their marketing site in git. It is proactive: it suggests the next thing to build. Examples include de-anonymization, landing pages, warmed emails, blog automation and agent telemetry. How does Letterpress-1 work? Letterpress-1 runs in 3 modes : Build: create a page or feature from a prompt, with brand copy and visuals kept consistent. Plan: pick a goal and get a build plan of growth actions. Fix: find site issues and dispatch pull requests to fix them. Every change follows the same loop. The agent reads the site, plans and builds in a sandbox. It reviews its own change, then opens a pull request. Each change returns a preview link of your own site . Nothing lands until you choose a preview, a pull request, or a merge after checks pass. Letter team lists 6 surfaces. These are the web platform, a Slack app, the letterpress CLI and a website portal. A standalone app and your own agent round out the list. The in-site IDE works on a live page. Press ⌘L, edit text where you see it, and a pull request follows. Showcase examples also cover A/B tests from live edits. For developers, agents.md documents an MCP server at app.letterstory.com/api/mcp with OAuth. The MCP manifest, OpenAPI spec and API reference form 1 registry of 760 tools. Claude Code, Codex or any MCP-capable agent can call the same functions the app uses. What are Proofs, Simulations, Benches and Phantoms? The launch post highlights 4 primitives aimed at winning over AI agents as buyers: Proofs: signed evidence of customer success, built from telemetry and billing data, for agent visitors. Simulations: mirror versions of your API or MCP with simulated data, so agents can try before buying. Benches: self-hosted, reproducible benchmark apps with open-source code and independent governance. Phantoms: independent, autonomous blogs used to sandbox growth strategies. The site adds more: Kernels, Letterbases, Visitors and Mailers. Then it watches competitor sitemaps and flag new pages. Letter team positions these as replacements for tools like G2, Semrush, Profound, RB2B and Instantly. newContent: MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ An Artificial Intelligence News Platform Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:51:09 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 https://www.marktechpost.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/cropped-Favicon-512-x-512-1-1-32x32.png MarkTechPost https://www.marktechpost.com/ 32 32 127842392 OpenAI Introduces Pando: A Git Backend That Cuts Median Push Latency ~80% https://www.marktechpost.com/2026/11/02/openai-pando-git-backend-monorepo/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 05:51:06 +0000 https://www.marktechpost.com/?p=83732 OpenAI built Pando, a Git-compatible backend for its monorepo. It handles branches independently, reuses stored packfiles across fetches, cut median push latency by nearly 80%, and now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. The post OpenAI Introduces Pando: A Git Backend That Cuts Median Push Latency ~80% appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> OpenAI has introduced Pando , a new Git backend that now serves all development in its monorepo. The OpenAI Pando Git backend keeps the standard Git client and protocol. Engineers and Codex agents still run git push and git fetch as before. Only the server changed. OpenAI team reports median push latency fell nearly 80%. Pando now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. TL;DR Scale: Nearly 1 PB of Git data per day; peak above 57 TB in 1 hour. Runs on: Commodity hardware; standard cloud VMs saturate 10 Gbps links on clone and fetch. Performance: Thousands of concurrent pushers without degradation, per OpenAI’s own testing. Best: Median push latency down nearly 80% (about 5x). Worst: Not open source; repeat branch pushes resend non-trunk history (p99 pack under 3 MiB). What is OpenAI Pando? Pando is a Git-compatible server backend from OpenAI that scales concurrent pushes and fetches for a monorepo. It was written in Rust and reached production in 10 weeks. One engineer designed the core and teams of Codex agents implemented it. It has served production traffic since April 2026. Why did OpenAI need a new Git backend? Codex multiplied parallel work. OpenAI’s commit chart shows commits landed on master up 1,378% in Q3 2026 versus Q1 2024. Its Q4 2026 estimate is +2,442%. Each push now triggers many CI fetches. By late 2025, fetches and pushes slowed, merges failed, and reliability at times fell below 90%. OpenAI concluded the bottleneck was how it served Git, not Git itself. How does Pando work? Pando drops 2 assumptions that most Git servers treat as requirements: 1. Repository-wide consistency : Conventional servers order every ref update repo-wide, so unrelated pushes wait. Pando uses causal consistency instead. Each branch is serialized on its own, and clients only conflict when pushing the same ref. The tradeoff: a reader viewing several branches may see them at different points in time. 2. A unique packfile per client : Standard servers build a fresh pack per fetch. Pando stores each pushed pack as an immutable blob. A “ref version” goes into a scalable metadata store. A push needs O(1) metadata reads and writes. A fetch needs O(log Δ) reads, where Δ is the ref-version gap to close. How are pushes kept small and reusable? With millions of branches, a full ref advertisement can exceed 100 MiB. Pando advertises only the trunk branch as the base for new feature-branch pushes. Any reader with trunk history can then fetch that branch from 1 stored pack. In OpenAI’s monorepo, the median pack was under 20 KiB. How are fetches served at line rate? Pando returns download links via packfile-uri , an existing Git protocol feature. It sends an empty inline pack. A delivery service called Express caches packs regionally, using consistent hashing, with hit rates above 99%. What replaces garbage collection? Each push creates an “L0” pack. Background workers group packs into geometrically larger covers, similar to LSM-tree compaction. The monorepo currently uses covers up to L4. Covers act as a skip list, so pack selection runs in logarithmic time. What are the production numbers? All figures below are self-reported by OpenAI. Median push latency reduced by nearly 80%. Nearly 1 PB of Git data per day, using only a handful of CPU cores. Over 57 TB of packs served in a single hour, more than 99% from local disk cache. Clones and fetches saturate 10 Gbps links on standard cloud VMs. OpenAI also ran a 1,000-writer simulation against 3-phase-commit and write-ahead-log designs. It labels these teaching models, not benchmarks. How does Pando compare with other approaches? Pando first ran as a read- and write-through proxy, so traffic moved without downtime. OpenAI ships its own Git build to developer machines and the ChatGPT desktop app. What goes back to upstream Git? OpenAI fixed client handling of concurrent, interrupted and resumed pack downloads, and added packfile-uri tracing. Its build adds parallel pack indexing and “explicit haves.” Several fixes are upstream. The rest sit in a public patch tracker . What are the limitations? Pando is not open source; OpenAI team states that it is exploring ways to share the technology. Cross-branch reads have no single point-in-time snapshot. Repeat or stacked branch pushes resend everything outside trunk. The p99 pack was under 3 MiB. Every performance number is self-reported, with no independent benchmark yet. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Fri, 30 Oct 2026 19:36:42 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/q3-2026-charts-funding-amounts-vs-round-counts/ Mon, 02 Nov 2026 12:00:28 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94310 Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3. Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups. Large rounds dominate funding One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more. As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023. The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic . But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds. Deals keep falling even as dollars rise In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared. In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year. The early-stage slump Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low. It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups , with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips. Looking ahead Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom. A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure. But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:56:10 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/october-2026-global-startup-funding-strong-china-deepseek/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:00:44 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94315 Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek . The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion. The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding. Funding concentration Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital , Index Ventures and Lux Capital . DeepSeek ’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance , and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI . DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI , a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board . The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange. Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity. Other large rounds last month went to Axiom , which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp , which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent , which says it raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi , which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes , which raised a $1 billion Series A. AI-driven A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI , which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev. A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month. Exits The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX ’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion . On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber ’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion. Looking ahead With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds. The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time. The post OpenAI Introduces Pando: A Git Backend That Cuts Median Push Latency ~80% appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> OpenAI has introduced Pando , a new Git backend that now serves all development in its monorepo. The OpenAI Pando Git backend keeps the standard Git client and protocol. Engineers and Codex agents still run git push and git fetch as before. Only the server changed. OpenAI team reports median push latency fell nearly 80%. Pando now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. TL;DR Scale: Nearly 1 PB of Git data per day; peak above 57 TB in 1 hour. Runs on: Commodity hardware; standard cloud VMs saturate 10 Gbps links on clone and fetch. Performance: Thousands of concurrent pushers without degradation, per OpenAI’s own testing. Best: Median push latency down nearly 80% (about 5x). Worst: Not open source; repeat branch pushes resend non-trunk history (p99 pack under 3 MiB). What is OpenAI Pando? Pando is a Git-compatible server backend from OpenAI that scales concurrent pushes and fetches for a monorepo. It was written in Rust and reached production in 10 weeks. One engineer designed the core and teams of Codex agents implemented it. It has served production traffic since April 2026. Why did OpenAI need a new Git backend? Codex multiplied parallel work. OpenAI’s commit chart shows commits landed on master up 1,378% in Q3 2026 versus Q1 2024. Its Q4 2026 estimate is +2,442%. Each push now triggers many CI fetches. By late 2025, fetches and pushes slowed, merges failed, and reliability at times fell below 90%. OpenAI concluded the bottleneck was how it served Git, not Git itself. How does Pando work? Pando drops 2 assumptions that most Git servers treat as requirements: 1. Repository-wide consistency : Conventional servers order every ref update repo-wide, so unrelated pushes wait. Pando uses causal consistency instead. Each branch is serialized on its own, and clients only conflict when pushing the same ref. The tradeoff: a reader viewing several branches may see them at different points in time. 2. A unique packfile per client : Standard servers build a fresh pack per fetch. Pando stores each pushed pack as an immutable blob. A “ref version” goes into a scalable metadata store. A push needs O(1) metadata reads and writes. A fetch needs O(log Δ) reads, where Δ is the ref-version gap to close. How are pushes kept small and reusable? With millions of branches, a full ref advertisement can exceed 100 MiB. Pando advertises only the trunk branch as the base for new feature-branch pushes. Any reader with trunk history can then fetch that branch from 1 stored pack. In OpenAI’s monorepo, the median pack was under 20 KiB. How are fetches served at line rate? Pando returns download links via packfile-uri , an existing Git protocol feature. It sends an empty inline pack. A delivery service called Express caches packs regionally, using consistent hashing, with hit rates above 99%. What replaces garbage collection? Each push creates an “L0” pack. Background workers group packs into geometrically larger covers, similar to LSM-tree compaction. The monorepo currently uses covers up to L4. Covers act as a skip list, so pack selection runs in logarithmic time. What are the production numbers? All figures below are self-reported by OpenAI. Median push latency reduced by nearly 80%. Nearly 1 PB of Git data per day, using only a handful of CPU cores. Over 57 TB of packs served in a single hour, more than 99% from local disk cache. Clones and fetches saturate 10 Gbps links on standard cloud VMs. OpenAI also ran a 1,000-writer simulation against 3-phase-commit and write-ahead-log designs. It labels these teaching models, not benchmarks. How does Pando compare with other approaches? OpenAI Pando GitHub Spokes Anthropic Scion Git client compatible Yes Yes No, own scn client Write coordination Per-branch, causal consistency Three-phase commit with quorum Server-side commits; refs via compare-and-swap Default replicas Not disclosed (blob + metadata stores) 5 full copies No fully materialized repo copy Read path Reused packs via packfile-uri, Express cache Closest in-sync replica Tiered tree/blob caches Cache hit rate Over 99% Not disclosed Over 99% per tier Headline result Median push latency down ~80% Serves ~1 billion repositories 200x smaller CPU/memory footprint Build effort 10 weeks, Rust Not disclosed 7 people, 5 months Available to others No Yes, powers GitHub No How was Pando built and deployed? OpenAI wrote a Git conformance suite for agents and added deterministic simulation testing. Agents using GPT-6 Astra wrote Lean and TLA+ specs to find bugs. Pando first ran as a read- and write-through proxy, so traffic moved without downtime. OpenAI ships its own Git build to developer machines and the ChatGPT desktop app. What goes back to upstream Git? OpenAI fixed client handling of concurrent, interrupted and resumed pack downloads, and added packfile-uri tracing. Its build adds parallel pack indexing and “explicit haves.” Several fixes are upstream. The rest sit in a public patch tracker . What are the limitations? Pando is not open source; OpenAI team states that it is exploring ways to share the technology. Cross-branch reads have no single point-in-time snapshot. Repeat or stacked branch pushes resend everything outside trunk. The p99 pack was under 3 MiB. Every performance number is self-reported, with no independent benchmark yet. Key Takeaways Pando keeps Git, but rebuilds the server for parallel agent traffic. Per-branch causal consistency removes repository-wide write contention. Stored, reusable packs replace per-client pack generation. Median push latency dropped nearly 80%; daily traffic nears 1 PB. Client fixes go upstream; the backend stays internal for now. On Ant Group inclusionAI's 124B Ling-3.0-flash, GSM8K decode throughput rose 42.5% with no detectable accuracy change. The post NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5% appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> NVIDIA’s latest technical blog shows how to speed up mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on one DGX Spark . The test model is Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash , a 124B-parameter MoE with 5.1B active parameters. NVIDIA stacked three optimizations: a new MoE kernel backend, an FP8 output layer and built-in speculative decoding. On all 1,319 GSM8K questions, decode throughput rose 42.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change. So why is it relevant for Devs? DGX Spark is a desktop system, not a data center node. NVIDIA’s results show a 124B MoE serving single-user requests faster on that desk-side box. The technical post also shows where MoE decode time goes, and how to cut it. TL;DR Size: Ling-3.0-flash-fp4: 124B total, 5.1B active per token; 256K native context. Runs on: One NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified memory, 273 GB/s), batch size one. Performance: Three stacked optimizations lift GSM8K decode throughput from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens/s. Best: +42.5% throughput and -24.5% mean latency, with accuracy flat (96.89% vs 96.82%). Lagging: Synthetic gains (+185.1%) shrink on GSM8K as MTP acceptance drops from 3.90 to 2.68. Why is MoE decoding on DGX Spark memory-bound? DGX Spark is NVIDIA’s desktop system built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. It offers 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Peak compute is up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4. NVIDIA rates it for inference on models up to 200B parameters. In the NVIDIA technical post , the NVIDIA team profiled Ling-3.0-flash-fp4 at batch size 1. Decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out, the MoE computation and the LM head that scores the vocabulary. That points to two levers: move fewer bytes per decode step, and generate more tokens per verification round. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe. It used FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 LM-head path. On a synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output test, it ran at 27.71 ms per token (36.09 tokens per second). What are the 3 optimizations? 1. Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels: NVIDIA swapped FlashInfer’s MoE backend for Humming , an independent kernel library. Humming uses NVRTC to compile kernels at runtime for the actual matrix shapes, data types and GPU. That includes the narrow 768-wide expert layer. Each kernel compiles in seconds. The FlashInfer CUTLASS path compiles 97 targets with ninja, on the order of tens of minutes. Throughput rose 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second. 2. Online FP8 LM head: The LM head is a 157,184 x 2,560 matrix stored in BF16. Every generated token reads all of it. Quantizing only this layer to FP8 at load time halves those reads. Setting SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1 enables it. It cannot be combined with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option. Combined with Humming, throughput reached 43.94 tokens per second. That is 21.7% over baseline and 11.4% over Humming alone. 3. MTP speculative decoding with NEXTN: Ling-3.0-flash ships with a built-in NEXTN prediction layer, so no extra draft model is needed. It drafts three tokens, and the model verifies four positions at once. Verification costs about 2.26x a normal decode step. The main cost is MoE, not attention. Verifying four tokens can activate up to 32 experts instead of 8. On the synthetic test, an average of 3.90 tokens were accepted per round. Throughput jumped to 102.88 tokens per second, up 185.1%. The three techniques do not overlap. Humming and the FP8 LM head cut the cost of each step. MTP cuts the number of steps. The integration trap: Stacking these is not automatic. With FP8 LM head and MTP both on, the draft must share the full LM-head module. Otherwise the framework silently falls back, and the draft interprets FP8 weights as BF16. Accept length drops to 1.00, and throughput falls below the unoptimized baseline. The NVIDIA team advises checking at startup that each optimization is active. NVIDIA points to the Ling cookbook notebook for enabling both together. What happens on a real workload? Synthetic tests flatter speculative decoding, so the NVIDIA team also ran all 1,319 GSM8K questions. It used 5-shot prompting with chain-of-thought, temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95 and top_k 29. With all three optimizations, time per output token fell from 26.45 ms to 18.56 ms. Decode throughput rose 42.5%, from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens per second. Mean latency dropped 24.5%, from 15.21 to 11.49 seconds. Accuracy moved from 96.89% to 96.82%, a change NVIDIA calls statistically undetectable. Accept length here was 2.68, versus 3.90 on synthetic data. The NVIDIA team gives three reasons for the gap. Synthetic outputs are more repetitive, so drafts are accepted more often. The synthetic test used greedy decoding, while GSM8K used sampling. GSM8K answers are also short, with a median near 310 tokens versus a fixed 2K.  What is Ling 3.0, and why does it suit DGX Spark? Ling-3.0-flash belongs to Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling 3.0 family , released under the MIT license. The open-weight lineup also includes Ling-3.0-tiny , a 7.9B MoE with 1.3B active parameters. Both come with base checkpoints and FP8, INT4 and GGUF builds; flash also has FP4. OpenRouter also lists inclusionAI’s vision-language, finance and health variants built on Ling 3.0 Flash. Ling-3.0-flash is built to keep per-token cost low: Sparse MoE: Each MoE layer routes a token to 8 of 512 routed experts , along with 1 shared expert. About 4.1% of the weights are active per token. Hybrid linear attention: 35 Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers and 7 Gated MLA layers alternate 5:1. KDA, from Moonshot AI’s Kimi Linear paper , keeps a fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache. The layout is native from the start of pretraining. Built-in MTP: The model was trained with multi-token prediction. That NEXTN layer is the draft model NVIDIA used. Agent focus: inclusionAI team reports 10,000+ interactive training environments for coding, general and deep-research agents. NVIDIA notes the native 256K context expands to 1M tokens. How strong and efficient is Ling-3.0-flash? On its model card , inclusionAI reports 56.6 on SWE-Bench Pro and 72.4 on SWE-Bench Multilingual. It also reports 93.2 on MathArena AIME 2026 and 87.0 on HMMT Feb 2026. Artificial Analysis results shown on OpenRouter list 85.5% on GPQA Diamond and 55.4% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The hardest reasoning tests remain tough: Humanity’s Last Exam scores 22.7 self-reported and 23.7% independently. API pricing: Artificial Analysis lists InclusionAI’s API at $0.075 per 1M input tokens and $0.22 per 1M output tokens. We’re actively recruiting a Senior CRM Manager as we continue to scale at M-KOPA. Most senior growth hires get one channel and one pod for years. This role is built differently: you’ll own two of our core growth pods in your first year, then land where you’ve had the most impact. It’s a fast track to pod leadership, not a support seat.</strong></p><p></p><div></div><p></p><h2>The Impact 💚</h2><p>You’ll drive the conversion growth that turns customers into long-term, high-value ones, creating financial inclusion for Africa’s traditionally excluded. We’ve already helped over 10 million customers access over $2 billion in credit 🌍</p><p></p><div></div><p></p><p><strong>The Opportunity</strong></p><p></p><p>🏗️ Real ownership from day one. You'll be the one accountable for delivery in Repeat Phones, not shadowing or supporting someone else's plan.</p><p>🎒 Two growth motions, one year. You'll take on Digital Lending mid-way through, working directly with one of our strongest performers to understand cash loans end to end, then carry that pod solo for a defined stretch. Few people get this breadth this early.</p><p> 🧭 A defined path, not indefinite floating. You'll build real expertise in our two conversion pods first, then move into Lifecycle in the second half of next year, reporting to the Lifecycle CRM Lead once you're there. The destination is set. What you bring to it is up to you. 🌍 Work inside a proven CLV engine. M-KOPA has helped more than 10 million customers access over $2 billion in credit. You'll be executing inside systems that already work, not guessing at what might.</p><p></p><p><strong>What You'll Do </strong></p><p></p><p><strong>Phase 1</strong>: Repeat Phones. Take ownership of reactivation and upgrade campaigns in CleverTap, working closely with the Growth Lead there to understand what's driving the pod's numbers and where the next opportunity is. You'll be trusted to make real calls here, not just execute a checklist. </p><p><strong>Phase 2</strong>: Cross into Digital Lending. Work directly with the Digital Lending lead, one of our top performers, to understand cash loan growth end to end before taking it on yourself. </p><p><strong>Phase 3</strong>: Own Digital Lending. Carry primary responsibility for Digital Lending for a defined period, with the Repeat Phones lead available if you need a second opinion. </p><p><strong>Phase 4</strong>: Move into Lifecycle. In the second half of next year, join the Lifecycle pod full-time, reporting to the Lifecycle CRM Lead. You'll bring a year of hands-on conversion experience into a pod that's still being built, real currency for shaping what Lifecycle does next. Throughout all phases, you will:</p><ul><li><p>Build and run multi-channel campaigns (SMS, WhatsApp, push, in-app) in CleverTap against pod goals </p></li><li><p>Track funnel performance and flag drop-off points to the pod lead you're supporting</p></li><li><p>Run structured experiments (creative, audience, incentive, or timing) with clear hypotheses </p></li><li><p>Turn what works into documented playbooks the next person can pick up </p></li><li><p>Keep data quality and campaign tracking clean enough that leadership can trust the numbers</p></li></ul><p></p><p><strong>Key Metrics You'll Influence </strong></p><p>Repeat Phones: Reactivation rate, upgrade conversion %, unit economics per sale </p><p>Digital Lending: Approval → disbursement rate, digital loan volume, approval quality </p><p>Campaign ROI and payback period across both </p><p></p><p><strong>Your Environment </strong></p><p>💼 Tech Stack: CleverTap (primary), Looker Channels: WhatsApp, SMS, push, in-app messaging </p><p>Markets: Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, Ghana</p><p></p><p><strong>What You Need </strong></p><ul><li><p>5+ years in growth, performance, or lifecycle marketing, ideally in fintech, telco, or e-commerce, with real ownership over what a campaign or a pod achieved, not just involvement in it. </p></li><li><p>Judgment as much as skill. You can walk into a pod, understand what's working and why, and make calls on where to push, not just follow a brief. </p></li><li><p>Genuine appetite for pod leadership.
